2.0.0.en: 1 "Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah. 2 Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts; 3 Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born, and make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst. 4 And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms.

2.0.1.en: "Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah. Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts" [1-2].

2.0.2.en: Since God declared of this nation that it had committed adultery by leaving its true God to unite its heart with Baal, He could not call it His wife, for it had betrayed Him and He had divorced it; rather He calls it "their mother," in order to rouse it to repentance and to return to Him, on the collective level as well as on the personal level of each member in it.

2.0.3.en: And with all the evil it had done, the Lord opens His speech by the prophet, as He closes it, with the declaration of renewing the covenant with them, announcing that they are His people and the object of His mercy. In this spirit the Apostle Paul says: "Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved" (Rom 10:1).

2.0.4.en: To whom is the speech directed: "Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah"? Although Gomer the daughter of Diblaim bears Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, there is a small remnant in the midst of the people who are holy to God, or at least longing for a life holy to the Lord. To these God directs His speech, that they may open the doors of hope before their fallen brethren and declare that God longs to gather them so that they may become His people and that He may have mercy on them, but not without sanctification or striving, for He says: "Plead."

2.0.5.en: Let them plead with their mother, who lost her belonging to God and is no longer His wife because of her adultery and whoredom. It is a trial that takes place within the circle of the soul by the Holy Spirit, so that man judges himself before he is exposed on the great day of the Lord. Let each one say to himself: "Plead with your mother, plead," so that we judge ourselves before we are judged. May we not be silent about the corruption of the bride who belongs to the Lord, but let us repeat to ourselves what St. Basil the Great wrote to a fallen virgin: [If John rebuked boldly, even to death, when he saw a marriage that ought not to have been, how much more would his feelings be when he sees the violation of a marriage belonging to the Lord! You have cast off from you the yoke of divine union. You have fled from the holy bridal chamber of the true King. You have fallen into that corrupt, defiled ruin... Who would not grieve over such things, saying: "How is the faithful city become an harlot" (Isa 1:21)?!]

2.1.0.en: As for the purpose of this trial, it is: "let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts" [2]. For when we judge ourselves we remove shamelessness from our face, so that we are ashamed of our weakness and seek to be covered by His grace; then we hear our heavenly Bridegroom saying: "Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away. O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely" (Song 2:13-14). He grants us the power of His resurrection, saying: "Arise," so we die to every uncleanness that stained our face, and His divine traits appear in His eyes, glorified by His resurrection and adorned by the work of His Holy Spirit.

2.1.1.en: May He remove by His Holy Spirit the adulteries from between the breasts, that is, from within the heart, so that we may say to Him: "He shall lie all night betwixt my breasts" (Song 1:13), for the Holy One cannot lodge where adultery settles, for what fellowship hath light with darkness? and what concord hath the Lord Christ with Belial?

2.1.2.en: What does removing adultery from the breasts mean? If the heavenly Bridegroom has two breasts, which are the Old and New Testaments, they are also the breasts of the bride, as they are the book of the Church, so it is fitting for the bride to present them through her holy life in the Lord, and for no one to corrupt their message by his evil life, causing others to stumble from enjoying them as food for souls. In this sense St. Jerome wrote to the monk Pammachius, encouraging him to study the Holy Bible, saying: [Give him your breasts to suck from your pierced bosom, and let him rest in his inheritance (Ps 68:13).]

2.2.0.en: If we judge ourselves we are not judged, but if we are lax with ourselves in the matter of sin, we fall under this sentence: "Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born, and make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst. And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms" [3-4].

2.2.1.en: What does He mean by saying, "Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born," except that since she left Him by her own will, He does not compel her to be joined to Him, so she loses Him as the covering of her inner life? She rejects Him, so she loses Him as a robe of righteousness with which she is clothed, and she appears in her corrupt nature as on the day of her bodily birth, with nothing to cover her weakness. She has deprived herself, by herself, of the Lord Christ, whom we put on, as the Apostle Paul says: (Gal 3:27).

2.2.2.en: As for His saying, "make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst," it is because she rejects God, so she does not receive His Holy Spirit, who comes down upon our barren earth like rain to water it and makes its arid wilderness a fruitful paradise, so that she may say to her Bridegroom: "Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 4:16).

2.2.3.en: As for His saying, "And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms," it points to the fruit that springs in us from ourselves and not from our union with the heavenly Bridegroom; of this the Lord Christ said that every plant which His heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Mt 15:13), for it is a stranger to the Kingdom of God and deserves only to be burned! These works that are not of God are "children of whoredoms," while the works that are of God's planting are bound to Him, untouched by the evil one, but remain accompanying us throughout our eternity, as the Church says: "Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them" (Rev 14:13).

2.3.0.en: 5 "For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink. 6 Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths. 7 And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them: then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.

2.3.1.en: As God seeks His bride, threatening her if she refuses, or rather warning her lest she become naked and a wilderness and not enjoy His mercy, He reveals to her that what happens to her is not out of cruelty on His part but is the natural fruit of her leaving the truth, the secret of her life and her satisfaction, and her running after vanity, which offers nothing but death and deprivation.

2.3.2.en: He says: "For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink" [5]. He has made clear that the secret of her ruin is her adultery and her committing of shame, not in the general bodily sense, but committing it first inwardly in the heart, where she places her needs with them: they provide her food (my bread), her drink (my water), her clothing (my wool and my flax), her medicines (my oil), and her delight (my drink). This is spiritual adultery, where man leans on another than God, the Bridegroom of his soul, to ask from him his needs and find in him his satisfaction and pleasure. And as God works to bring us back to Himself, He tightens the pressure around us so that we realize that our running after others offers us nothing but a mirage, for He says: "Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths. And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them" [7]. If sin brings man "thorns also and thistles" (Gen 3:18), and as the wise man says: "Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward" (Prov 22:5), then God in His love lets these thorns block our way, that perhaps we may realize our error and return to Him. When it is said that God is froward with the froward (Ps 18:36), and "walk[s] contrary" to those who walk contrary to Him (Lev 26:23-24), He does so as the natural fruit of our evil, so that we reap the fruit of evil, and at the same time as a sign of divine love for our chastisement, that we may turn back from our way. If we do not care, He sets up for us a wall of afflictions and toils to close our crooked way before us, and we realize that our striving in it is vain.

2.3.3.en: Through this affliction we realize the vanity of our running after others, for we draw near to the lovers but do not overtake them, and we seek them but do not find them. Who are these lovers? Perhaps He meant by them the king of Assyria and the Pharaoh of Egypt and those like them, for an alliance with one of them for fear of another is a vain alliance, for these work for their own interest and exploit Israel and Judah without helping them in the time of distress. They are like "the staff of this bruised reed" (2 Kgs 18:21). Perhaps by the lovers He also meant Baal and Ashtaroth and the sorcery that accompanied idolatrous worship... all of which Israel dedicated its life, its energies and all its feelings to, although they cannot rescue or save it.

2.4.0.en: The purpose of these troubles is the return of the bride to her wise attachment, so that she leaves her adultery and returns to her true husband: "then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now" [7], as though she were the prodigal son who said: "I will arise and go to my father" (Lk 15:18).

2.5.0.en: 8 "For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal. 9 Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness. 10 And now will I discover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and none shall deliver her out of mine hand. 11 I will also cause all her mirth to cease, her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths, and all her solemn feasts. 12 And I will destroy her vines and her fig trees, whereof she hath said, These are my rewards that my lovers have given me: and I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall eat them. 13 And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD.

2.5.1.en: In our study of the book of Ezekiel we saw God rebuking His bride not only because she was unfaithful but because she took His riches and His holy things to use them in her betrayal of Him. Here God remarks that His bride takes His corn and His wine and His oil and His silver and His gold to offer them to Baal; she uses the divine gifts in the service of evil! We have already explained the symbols of these gifts and their spiritual meanings in some detail.

2.5.2.en: As for the fruit of this painful conduct, it is:

2.6.0.en: First: God withdraws His gifts at the proper time, for He says: "Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness" [9]. It is remarkable that God lets His bride do what she wishes with His gifts and talents, despite her misuse of them, that perhaps she may realize her error and return. But this leaving is for a time, for at the proper time He withdraws what He gave her, so she becomes hungry, thirsty and naked, exposed even before the eyes of her lovers. God is longsuffering toward us, but if we persist in misusing His gifts to us, He takes away what He gave us and makes us an example and a mockery even among the wicked, which the prophet Jeremiah realized when Jerusalem was taken captive, saying: "all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness: yea, she sigheth, and turneth backward. Her filthiness is in her skirts... she had no comforter" (Lam 1:8-9).

2.7.0.en: Second: She loses not only the gifts and talents but also her joy and her temporal and eternal peace, for He says: "I will also cause all her mirth to cease, her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths, and all her solemn feasts" [11]. He causes all her temporal joys to cease, and she enters into perpetual bitterness, gloom and distress, and knows no more joy or feast. But the believer, in the midst of bearing the cross, has his heart drawn to the joy of the resurrection and its power, and in the midst of sufferings he tastes inner rest on a heavenly level, and in the midst of sorrow he rejoices and no one can take his joy from him.

2.7.1.en: St. John Chrysostom affirms in more than one place that man's peace and joy spring from his depths within through the holy life in the Lord, and that his harm does not spring from external factors but from his sin, for he says: [For this reason I do not fear the plots of enemies, but I fear one thing, sin; I want to teach you a lesson, which is not to fear the deceptions of the powerful, but fear the power of sin. No one harms you if you do not harm yourself by yourself. If you do not sin, tens of thousands of swords threaten you, but God snatches you from them so that they do not come near you; but if you commit evil, even if you are inside paradise you will be driven out of it.]

2.8.0.en: Third: He destroys her vines and her fig trees [12]; we saw earlier in the introduction to this commentary the vine and the fig tree as symbols of the suffering Church, marked by unity of spirit. It is as though the man who leaves the Bridegroom of his soul loses the traits of the Church and his membership in it, and even becomes a forest eaten by the beasts of the field [12], that is, prey for Satan and a table for sin.

2.9.0.en: Fourth: The end of all this is her receiving divine punishment, "And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD" [13]. God reckons with her exactly, because she offered incense to the idols of Baal and adorned herself for them with earrings and jewels and went after her lovers committing debauchery with them and left God, the fountain of holiness. She offered incense as a sign of prayer and refuge to Baal, and adorned herself for him as a sign of the desire to please him and be united with him, and ran after the lovers as an indication of the attachment of the heart. Thus she offered all her capacities to Baal and not to her Bridegroom, whom she had utterly forgotten, so she deserved to fall under eternal punishment.

2.10.0.en: 14 "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her. 15 And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt. 16 And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me my husband; and shalt call me no more Baali. 17 For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name. 18 And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely. 19 And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. 20 I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD. 21 And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith the LORD, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth; 22 And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel. 23 And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people; and he shall say, Thou art my God."

2.10.1.en: After declaring the evil that the unfaithful bride committed and her squandering of her Bridegroom's wealth on behalf of His enemy, revealing the fruits of this vain conduct, He returns in tenderness and gentleness to declare His desire for her return to Him, for He says: "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her" [14].

2.10.2.en: What bridegroom speaks tenderly to his bride after her betrayal of him and her squandering of his possessions on another? So God longs for man, allures him and speaks tenderly to him, that perhaps he may return to Him and accept union with Him. And since God sanctifies human freedom, He does not compel him to return, but allures him to draw him to Himself, to lead him into the wilderness, where he finds no helper but God alone, who speaks tenderly to him in the wilderness as He spoke tenderly to the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai, offering them all love and showing them all tenderness and care.

2.11.s.en: And now, with what does God speak tenderly to her so that she may return to Him?

2.11.0.en: First: "I will give her her vineyards from thence" [15]; for although He takes her into the wilderness, He gives her her vineyards there in the wilderness, and vineyards provide food (grapes), drink (grape juice) and gladdening wine. What are these vineyards that the Lord gives her but Himself, for He says: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman" (Jn 15:1), as though He offers His life for satisfaction, refreshment and joy; she enjoys Him as the Bread that came down from heaven (Jn 6:50), and drinks from Him as the living fountain (Jer 2:13), and is made drunk with His love, saying: "Thy love is better than wine" (Song 1:2).

2.11.1.en: Although the world has become like a barren wilderness that cannot offer us anything, yet in the world we find the true vine come down to us that we may possess it, indeed that we may abide in it as branches and bring forth much fruit (Jn 15:5), and this is the secret of our joy and the exultation of our hearts in the midst of the wilderness of this world.

2.12.0.en: Second: "And I will give her... the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt" [15].

2.12.1.en: It is remarkable that when God takes her into the wilderness and offers Himself to her as "vineyards," she receives with the vineyards distress, for the word "Achor" means (trouble) or (affliction), and it is a valley in which Achar (Achan) the son of Zerah was stoned (Josh 7:26), about ten miles south of Jericho. He who receives the Lord Christ in the wilderness of this world receives Him as the satisfaction of his soul, but not without distress, and as St. John Chrysostom says, where Christ is, there also is the antichrist, resisting Him.

2.12.2.en: "Achor" is God's gift... "I will give her the valley of Achor," and as the Apostle Paul says of the gift of suffering: "For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake" (Phil 1:29), and as St. John Chrysostom says: [He lifts up our souls, counting these sufferings as His own; what joy fills us to be partakers with Christ, and to suffer for His sake!], [As He suffered from men, we too suffer with Him... therefore it is fitting for you not to be troubled by these sufferings but rather to rejoice in them.]

2.12.3.en: It is remarkable that God gives us "the valley of Achor for a door of hope," for in the midst of suffering the door of hope opens before us, as we taste the power of the resurrection and its joy through the cross with the Lord Christ, so we return to our renewed youth, and our tongue is opened in exultation, and our life is turned into an inner song of joy: "and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt" [15].

2.13.0.en: Third: She enjoys union with the heavenly Bridegroom: "And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me my husband; and shalt call me no more Baali" [16], that is, she accepts union with God without using the pagan language (Baali, that is, my master or my lord); He sanctifies her completely even in her words, for He says: "For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name."

2.14.0.en: She enters with Him into a marriage covenant that sanctifies her body and her mind and grants her surpassing peace even at her passing from this world. "And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely" [18]. What is "that day" but the day of the coming of the Lord Christ and His being lifted up on the cross for our salvation, where He offered His shed blood as a new covenant, through which our sanctification is accomplished, so that the beasts of the field within us become tame, and the fowls of heaven, that is, the mind, become holy, and even the creeping things of the ground, that is, the lowest bodily energies, are blessed in Him, breaking by His cross the bow of sin and the sword of the devil and removing the battle from the body (the earth), as body and soul become sanctified in Him, and making even our lying down in the grave safe, where hell cannot seize us nor death corrupt our peace!

2.15.0.en: The secret of this divine work in our life is His saying, affirming it three times, "I will betroth thee unto me" [19-20], and He affirms "unto me," for God gives us Himself, and as St. John Chrysostom says to the Church in the words of the Lord Christ: [I promise you the Kingdom... yes, I have given you the greatest portion, I have given you even the Lord of the Kingdom!.

2.16.s.en: As for the features of this heavenly betrothal, they are:

2.16.0.en: a. "I will betroth thee unto me for ever," an eternal betrothal that time cannot dissolve nor death corrupt... its foundation is the love that many waters cannot quench (Song 8:7)!

2.16.1.en: b. "I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies" [19]. What are righteousness, judgment and love but the person of the Lord Christ, who came down to us so that mankind might enjoy the bride in Him! Through Him the Father came to us to carry us in His arms, and in Him we come before the Father as a bride for the only-begotten Son, having the right of sonship to Him and union with Him. By our union with the heavenly Bridegroom we bear His traits, that is, righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness and mercies, and we become heavenly, as St. John Chrysostom says: [Consider what the Spirit has done. He found the earth full of demons and made it heaven.]

2.17.0.en: c. "I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD" [20]. The foundation of the betrothal is faith, by which we are united with the Bridegroom, and He leads us to His Father and we come to know Him, not with the purely dry knowledge of the mind but with the knowledge of life and union, which the Lord Himself had earlier declared: "neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him" (Mt 11:27). If union with Baal bears the fruit of ignorance of God, then union with the Son has as its aim entering into the Father's bosom and knowing Him closely and cleaving to Him!

2.18.0.en: Fourth: "And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith the LORD, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth" [21]. What are the heavens but the soul that bears the Lord Christ within it as its Bridegroom? The Father answers the soul united with the heavenly Bridegroom, for He smells in it the fragrance of good pleasure and it is the object of His delight. As for the earth, that is, the body, it is also sanctified with the soul and no longer resists God's work but becomes an instrument of righteousness working on His behalf; therefore the Lord hears this holy earth in which righteousness dwells. The earth no longer resists heaven, nor does the body wrestle with the holy soul, but responds to it and bears the fruits of the Spirit, which are from the sowing of God Himself: "And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel" [22].

2.19.0.en: Finally God concludes the blessings of this Messianic age, in which man returns to his Bridegroom, affirming the surpassing grace of God to us, saying: "And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people; and he shall say, Thou art my God" [23]. God's own hand reaches out to sow us, so that we are no longer without mercy nor are we any longer not His people, but we enjoy His mercy and belonging to Him and take pride in His divinity.

2.19.1.en: "Jezreel" has become a promise after it was a threat, and has become a sign of God who sows His Church by Himself, after it was a sign of the vineyard seized by the wicked Jezebel. As for His promise: "I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people," the Apostle Paul quoted it in his Epistle to the Romans as a prophecy about the calling of the Gentiles, who were not pitied and not the people of God, saying: "As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved" (Rom 9:25).
